title: Living ashtpadi 19

cards: Every home has one. The drawer. Dead batteries, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed, three keys to locks nobody remembers, a charger for a phone long gone.
Nobody decided to keep any of it. It just collected, the way things do when nobody's looking. And every time you open that drawer looking for scissors, you have to dig.
The nineteenth ashtpadi has spent three days on what stays behind and what goes along. Living it starts somewhere very small. Maybe with that drawer.

teach.b: Here's the nineteenth ashtpadi in one breath: the riches, youth and power we pile up stay behind; the Name we earn and the good we do go along. So how do people actually live that? Not, in Sikh teaching, by leaving home.
Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, raising a family, running a community kitchen. Sikhs call that life grihasti, the householder's path, and hold it up as a full spiritual life.

So living light doesn't mean owning nothing. It means owning lightly, holding things with an open hand. Guru Nanak gave a picture for it in the Sidh Gosht, his conversation with the Siddhas, the yogi masters.

teach.h: THE LOTUS: IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED.
teach.b: In paraphrase: as the lotus floats on the water and stays untouched by it, as the duck swims the stream and stays dry. Kamal, the lotus: it lives in the pond and isn't soaked by it. In the world, not drowned in it.

It may seem silly to link a junk drawer to a hymn, but Sukhmani works on the mind, and the mind is often cluttered in exactly that way: old grudges, worries about things that never happened, plans for a life you outgrew.
Clearing a drawer won't clear all that. But it's practice. You learn to look at something, admit you're not using it, and let it go to someone who will.
That's living light: not empty hands, open ones.

how: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life, grihasti, and Guru Nanak's picture of the lotus untouched by the water is used for living in the world without being owned by it.

o: the lotus, in the water but untouched by it
a garland of flowers offered in prayer
a temple bell rung at every sunrise

p: in the water, not soaked by it

s: living light means Sikhs should give up home and family
the Gurus honored the householder's life; Guru Nanak farmed and raised a family.
Guru Nanak's picture for living in the world is a lotus on the water
it floats in the pond and stays untouched by it.
the junk drawer is an image from Sukhmani itself
it's today's practice ground; Sukhmani works on the clutter of the mind.

games.q: you've taken Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi to heart. what does the Sikh tradition point you toward?
o: leave home and everything in it behind.
keep your life, but hold it with an open hand.
hold on tighter, since it all goes anyway.
games.why: Guru Nanak's last years were the householder's path: farm, family, kitchen, and giving. living light means open hands, not empty ones.

practice: Go to the drawer if you can, or picture it clearly, and take out one thing at a time, holding each for a breath: do I use this, could someone else?
Make three small piles, keep, give, throw away, without hurrying and without judging yourself for what's in there. If you pray, say Waheguru as each thing goes.

wordCard.voice: Kamal, the lotus: the householder's way is owning lightly, like the kamal on the water, untouched by it, and letting go of what you don't use so it can move on.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kamal, the lotus, Guru Nanak's picture in the Sidh Gosht for living in the world untouched by it.

carryVoice: Your line: live light. The lotus lives in the pond and stays dry. Day five hundred thirteen.
